OF THOMAS MORE'S UTOPIA

it is for the dignity of a ruler to exercise authority over beggars, but rather over the wealthy and fortunate. Indeed, Fabricius, a man of an upright and lofty spirit, surely understood this when he replied that he would rather rule over rich men than be rich himself. And in truth, for one person to wallow in pleasure and luxury while others everywhere are groaning and lamenting is to be the jailer, not the ruler, of a kingdom. Finally, just as a most unskilled physician is one who knows not how to cure one disease except by another, so he who does not know how to reform the life of his citizens except by taking away the comforts of life should admit that he does not know how to rule over free men. Rather, let him cast off his own sloth or arrogance; for it is usually through these vices that the people either despise him or hold him in hatred. Let him live innocently upon his own resources, let him adapt his expenses to his revenues, let him curb wrongdoing, and by the right training of his people, let him prevent evils from growing rather than allow them to increase only to punish them later. Let him not rashly revive laws abrogated by custom, especially those which, having been long neglected, were never missed. Nor should he ever accept, in the name of a transgression, anything of a kind that a judge would not allow a private citizen to accept, regarding it as dishonest and cunning. Here, if I were to propose to them the law of the Macarenses, who themselves are not very far from Utopia, whose king, on the first day he begins his reign, after great sacrifices, is bound by an oath never to hold at one time more than a thousand pounds of gold in his treasury, or an equivalent amount in silver. <margin>The remarkable law of the Macarenses</margin>

<summary>More argues that a true king secures his authority by managing the welfare of his subjects rather than impoverishing them, and he cites the restrictive wealth laws of the Macarenses as an ideal model of governance.</summary>
